2022_282_m092022bdmtg.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held September 20, 2022 at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:00 p.m. with Trustee Hauff absent and approximately 80 people in the audience. Ahead of the November 8, 2022 bond election, the Board adopted resolution 22-074 appointing TMP Architecture, Inc. as architect/engineer, Barton Malow Builder LLC as construction manager and Lecole Planners, L.L.C. as owner's representative, with compensation expressly contingent on issuance of General Obligation Unlimited Tax Bonds. **Meeting**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, September 20, 2022, Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present: Schmidt, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Philippart, Wilson. Absent: Hauff. Also present: Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Fulcher, Brinks, Griffin, Milanov, Roncone and West. Approximately 80 members of the audience. Adjourned 9:15 p.m. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary.

**Recognitions**
- 2022-2023 student representatives introduced: Alexi Papadelis (Troy College & Career High School), Yara Mashal (International Academy-East), Sara Ali (Athens High School), Nishit "Nish" Palepu (Troy High School).
- Sixteen all-state athletes from the 2022 spring sports season recognized by Mr. Fulcher.
- Brian Miska, Troy High coach, named MHSCA Boys' Tennis Coach of the Year; award to be presented November 13 in Lansing.
- Summer Learning Lab at Boulan Park using the Stanford Design Thinking Process, presented by Angela Milanov and teacher Philip Lewan with students Sara Chittala, Sejal Dash and Victor Zhong.
- Troy High Media Center named a 2022/2023 Model 21st Century School Library for Michigan; Media Specialist Toni Isaac recognized for service to Troy High's 2,100 students; awards banquet in Ann Arbor on November 10.
- MASB honors: Nicole Wilson, Award of Distinction & Advocacy Skills Specialty (all Level 3 courses and a minimum of 208 education credits); Gary Hauff, 24 Years of Service; the Board, Standard of Excellence Award.

**Resolution 22-071 - National Suicide Prevention Month**
Moved by Philippart, supported by Hammond, at the request of Oakland Community Health Network. Cited figures: 45,979 U.S. suicide deaths in 2020, one death every 11 minutes; 12.2 million adults seriously considered suicide, 3.2 million made a plan, 1.2 million attempted; the 2020 Michigan Suicide Prevention Commission Annual Report counted 1,389 Michigan suicide deaths during the pandemic, 1,099 of them men. References the new 988 dialing code and the #BeThere campaign. Adopted, Yes 6, No 0, Absent Hauff.

**Board actions**

| Item | Action | Vote |
|---|---|---|
| 22-072 | Consent agenda A-C: August 16, 2022 minutes; Treasurer's Report - July 2022; first reading of 15 revised policies plus new Policy 5000.05 | 6-0, Hauff absent |
| 22-073 | Personnel recommendations, new hires | 6-0, Hauff absent |
| 22-074 | Bond service providers: TMP Architecture, Barton Malow Builder LLC, Lecole Planners, L.L.C. | 6-0, Hauff absent |
| 22-075 | Cafeteria tables, Costello Elementary, School Specialty, $58,803.36, Community Education Fund | 6-0, Hauff absent |
| 22-076 | MASB 2022 Delegate Assembly delegates | 6-0, Hauff absent |

**Staffing and curriculum**
Jordan Harris, Assistant Superintendent for Employee Services, reported the District hired 41 new teachers and outlined administrative changes. He told Dr. Philippart the applicant pool has fallen from over 400 applicants five to six years ago to 200, and told Mrs. Anne that recent legislation lets retired educators return after nine months with no restrictions. Kris Griffor and Christine DiPilato presented on summer professional learning and summer school, including the TSD Literacy Project with over 100 teachers, Littera Tutoring, Math Recovery, and four Summer Literacy Meet-Ups in Troy parks for K-5 families.

**Public comment and announcements**
Eight speakers addressed homework policy, school investment, inclusion, sixth-grade curriculum materials, and the bond; three announced Board candidacies. Dr. Machesky noted bond Community Conversations beginning at the Troy Public Library and a League of Women Voters "Meet the Candidate Night" on October 6.

2022_283_troy_sd_comments.paragraph: Review comments dated January 28, 2022 from the Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting review team on the Troy School District's annual financial report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2021. The review team's consensus was to award the Certificate of Excellence, commending the District for its efforts, while listing nine technical comments on the financial and statistical sections. The most substantive concerns terminology of "reserved" versus restricted fund balance, classification of inventory as nonspendable, and the $1,425,000 of debt fund moneys deposited with the bond refunding escrow agent, which should be reported as a debt service expenditure rather than an other financing use.

Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting review comments issued January 28, 2022 for the Troy School District, Troy, MI, covering the fiscal year ended June 30, 2021. The opening determination states: "It is the consensus of the review team to award the Certificate of Excellence (COE). The School District is to be commended for its efforts." The remainder of the document is organized as a comment table keyed to page references in the District's report, split between a Financial Section and a Statistical Section, followed by a courtesy listing of GASB pronouncements the District should consider in preparing future reports.

FINANCIAL SECTION COMMENTS.

Page 7: The fourth paragraph mentions "reserved" fund balance, which should be changed to restricted to be consistent with page 12 and GASB Statement 54.

Pages 12 and 48: Regarding the nonspendable fund balance in the Nonmajor Governmental Funds (page 12) and the Food Service Fund (page 48), it is unclear why the inventory balance is reported as nonspendable rather than restricted. Fund balances representing inventory held for resale should not be classified as nonspendable if the proceeds from the sales are restricted, committed, or assigned. Authority cited: Q&A 54.46.

Pages 14 and 68: As disclosed on page 31, $1,425,000 of debt fund moneys were deposited with the bond refunding escrow agent. When a government uses its own resources, rather than proceeds of new borrowings, to fund an escrow account, that payment should be reported as a debt service expenditure as opposed to an other financing use in a governmental fund. Authority cited: Cod. Sec. D20.123.

Page 28: The notes should disclose amounts (emphasis added in the original) transferred from other funds by individual major fund and nonmajor funds in the aggregate. Authorities cited: GASBS 38: 15a; 2012 GAAFR, page 384; eGAAFR, page 506.

Page 31: Regarding the "Thereafter" line in the debt service table, debt service payments for subsequent periods should be reported in at least five-year increments rather than in total. Authorities cited: NCGA-I6: 4h; GASBS 38: 10; 2012 GAAFR, page 376; eGAAFR, page 499.

Notes (general): The notes should include a general description of prior period advance refundings of debt, and the amount of in substance defeased debt that remains outstanding as of the balance sheet date. Authorities cited: GASBS 7: 14; 2012 GAAFR, page 378; eGAAFR, page 501.

Notes (general): Regarding the net pension liability and net OPEB liability, which are reported as long-term liabilities, the notes should disclose changes in long-term liability balances during the period. Authorities cited: GASBS 34: 199; 2012 GAAFR, page 375; eGAAFR, page 499.

STATISTICAL SECTION COMMENT.

Page 60: The first paragraph should be reworded to refer to the "annual comprehensive financial report" to be consistent with the rest of the report.

GASB STATEMENTS PROVIDED AS A COURTESY. The reviewers note that the school district should consider the effects of the following GASB Statements, as applicable, in preparing future Comprehensive Annual Financial Reports.

Statement No. 87, Leases, issued June 2017, establishes standards of accounting and financial reporting for leases by lessees and lessors. Originally effective for periods beginning after December 15, 2019; GASB Statement No. 95 allows governments to postpone implementation for 18 months.

Statement No. 89, Accounting for Interest Cost Incurred before the End of a Construction Period, issued June 2018, establishes accounting requirements for interest costs incurred before the end of a construction period. Originally effective for periods beginning after December 15, 2019; Statement No. 95 allows a one-year postponement.

Statement No. 91, Conduit Debt Obligations, issued May 2019, establishes a single method of reporting conduit debt obligations by issuers to eliminate diversity in practice. Originally effective for periods beginning after December 15, 2020; Statement No. 95 allows a one-year postponement.

Statement No. 92, Omnibus 2020, issued January 2020, addresses a variety of topics to enhance comparability in accounting and financial reporting and improve consistency of authoritative literature by addressing practice issues identified during implementation and application of certain GASB Statements. Originally effective for periods beginning after June 15, 2021; Statement No. 95 allows a one-year postponement.

Statement No. 93, Replacement of Interbank Offered Rates, issued March 2020, addresses accounting and financial reporting issues and implications resulting from the replacement of an interbank offered rate. Originally effective for periods beginning after June 15, 2020, June 15, 2021 and December 31, 2021 depending on the paragraph; Statement No. 95 allows a one-year postponement.

Statement No. 94, Public-Private and Public-Public Partnerships and Availability Payment Arrangements, issued March 2020, addresses issues related to public-private and public-public partnership arrangements (PPPs) and provides guidance for accounting and financial reporting for availability payment arrangements (APAs). Effective for periods beginning after June 15, 2022.

Statement No. 95, Postponements of Effective Dates of Certain Authoritative Guidance, issued May 2020, was issued to provide temporary relief to governments and other stakeholders in light of the COVID-19 pandemic. Its requirements were effective immediately.

Statement No. 96, Subscription-Based Information Technology Arrangements, issued May 2020, provides guidance on accounting and financial reporting for subscription-based information technology arrangements. Effective for periods beginning after June 15, 2022.

Statement No. 97, Certain Component Unit Criteria, and Accounting and Financial Reporting for Internal Revenue Code Section 457 Deferred Compensation Plans - An Amendment of GASB Statements No. 14 and No. 84, and a Supersession of GASB Statement No. 32, issued June 2020, provides guidance regarding financial reporting of defined contribution pension plans, defined contribution OPEB plans, and other employee benefit plans, and enhances information related to Section 457 plans that meet the definition of a pension plan and investment information for all Section 457 plans. Paragraphs 4 and 5 were effective immediately; the remaining requirements are effective for periods beginning after June 15, 2021.

Statement No. 98, The Annual Comprehensive Financial Report, issued October 2021, establishes the term annual comprehensive financial report and its acronym ACFR. Effective for fiscal years ending after December 15, 2021.

2022_284_updates_memo_open_meetings_act_.paragraph: Policy update memorandum from MJ School Policy Services to MJ Policy Service Clients, dated September 19, 2022, recommending a revision to Policy 1002 ("Meetings of the Board of Education") on electronic meetings and remote participation. The memo marks the July 2022 language outdated as of the 9/16/22 update and narrows the grounds for remote participation to military duty absence or reasonable accommodation for a disability, dropping medical condition and local state of emergency because the Open Meetings Act no longer permits those bases. Clients must choose between Option A, requiring physical presence, and Option B, which lets other members contribute remotely if not counted toward a quorum or allowed a deciding vote.
2022_284_updates_memo_open_meetings_act_.page:
**Memo**
TO: MJ Policy Service Clients. FROM: MJ School Policy Services. DATE: September 19, 2022. RE: Policy Manual Update - Open Meetings Act. Subject policy: 1002, "Meetings of the Board of Education," under the "Meeting Procedures" subheading. Questions directed to Policy@MillerJohnson.com.

**What changed**
The July 2022 MJ SPS update language, reproduced and marked "OUTDATED AS OF 9/16/22 UPDATE," had permitted remote participation necessitated by military duty, a medical condition, or a local state of emergency/disaster. Both new options permit remote participation only on the basis of (1) absence due to military leave or (2) reasonable accommodation required because of a disability. Medical condition and local state of emergency/disaster language was removed because the Open Meetings Act no longer permits remote participation on those bases. Under the OMA, only a board member absent due to military duty may - and in fact must - be permitted to attend remotely. Attorney General Nessel released an opinion letter earlier in the year providing that a board member with a disability must be accommodated where remote participation is the only reasonable accommodation available; the memo agrees that the Americans with Disabilities Act negates the OMA to the extent compliance with the OMA would require violating the ADA.

**The practical problem**
COVID-19-era amendments provide that remote participation is only permitted in accordance with the OMA, and the OMA explicitly allows remote participation only for military-duty absence. Taken to its logical extreme, board members could listen remotely but could not voice an opinion on a pending matter. Prior Attorney General opinions had generally accepted remote participation so long as such members were not used to establish a quorum or cast the deciding vote; the recent amendments call the continuing legitimacy of those opinions into question. The firm's position is that an argument remains that members may contribute remotely without a military or disability basis so long as they are not counted toward a quorum and not permitted to be a deciding vote, citing MCL 15.263a(1) and MCL 15.263a(8), while acknowledging the approach carries legal risk including potential payment of attorney's fees.

**Option A (lower risk)**
A Board member must be physically present to participate as a Board member, except as otherwise permitted by the OMA.

**Option B (more flexibility, more risk)**
A Board member must be physically present to be counted toward a quorum or vote. Members not explicitly authorized under the OMA and without a qualifying disability may remotely contribute, but may not be counted toward a quorum or vote. If any member is present remotely under an OMA-authorized reason or disability accommodation, no other member may contribute remotely unless they too qualify.

**Conditions common to both options** when a member participates remotely due to military duty or disability accommodation:
- Advance notice posted consistent with MCL 15.263a(4) and agenda posted consistent with MCL 15.263a(5), in addition to any other OMA notice;
- Board Secretary records the name of each member attending remotely in the minutes, with an announcement at the outset of the meeting; except for military-duty absence, the announcement must identify the member's specific location by state and city, township, county, or village;
- 2-way communication so remote members can hear and be heard by other members and public participants;
- The remote member notifies the Board President at least one business day before the meeting;
- The Board President ensures the public knows how any remote member voted, such as by requiring roll call voting.

Memorandum from MJ School Policy Services to MJ Policy Service Clients, dated September 19, 2022, regarding a Policy Manual Update on the Open Meetings Act. The memo contains a recommended update/modification to Policy 1002 ("Meetings of the Board of Education").

BACKGROUND. The MJ SPS July 2022 update had contained recommended updates/modifications to Policy 1002 under an "Electronic Meetings and Remote Participation" section below the "Meeting Procedures" subheading. That language, reproduced in full and labeled "OUTDATED AS OF 9/16/22 UPDATE," provided that remote participation in Board meetings should be limited to the extent possible; that Board members should be physically present and remote participants may not be used to constitute a quorum unless the remote participation is necessitated by military duty, a medical condition, or a local state of emergency/disaster, in accordance with the OMA. Its conditions required the Board Secretary to include the name of each Board member attending remotely in the meeting minutes; that the remote member hear and be heard by other Board members and those in attendance; that the remote member notify the Board President at least one (1) business day before the meeting so the President could arrange to notify the general public of the means by which it may contact the member prior to the meeting; and that the Board President take steps to ensure the general public is aware of the manner any remote member voted on all matters brought to a vote, such as by requiring roll call voting.

WHY THE CHANGE. The memo states this language created significant internal discussion within the MJ Education Law Team and additional requests for clarification from clients, several of whom sought guidance on the permissible level of Board member remote participation. As a result, the MJ Education Law Team presents two options. As an initial matter, both options now permit remote participation by board members only on the basis of (1) absence due to military leave or (2) reasonable accommodation required because of a disability. Language pertaining to a medical condition or local state of emergency/disaster has been removed because the Open Meetings Act ("OMA") no longer permits remote participation on those bases. At present, under the OMA, only a board member absent due to military duty may - and in fact must - be permitted to attend the meeting remotely. Additionally, Attorney General Nessel released an opinion letter earlier in the year providing that a board member with a disability must be accommodated, meaning that if the only reasonable accommodation available is remote participation, the member is entitled to it. A footnote states that the OMA does not contain language allowing for such an exception, but that, as AG Nessel argues and the firm agrees, the Americans with Disabilities Act ("ADA") negates the OMA to the extent following the OMA would require violating the ADA.

THE PRACTICAL CONCERN. The memo summarizes client concern: COVID-19-era amendments to the OMA provide that remote participation is only permitted in accordance with the OMA, and the OMA explicitly only allows remote participation if one is absent due to military duty. Taken to its logical extreme, this would prohibit board members from contributing to a board meeting in any way unless absent due to military leave; such members could listen remotely but could not voice an opinion on a pending board matter. Multiple clients expressed concern with this overly-strict language. Prior to the recent amendments, Attorney General opinions had given some guidance, and it was generally accepted that board members could participate remotely but generally advised that they not be used to establish a quorum or be the deciding vote on a motion. The recent amendments call the continuing legitimacy of those opinions into question.

THE FIRM'S POSITION. It remains the firm's position that there is an argument that board members may still contribute to board meetings remotely, even without a military duty absence or a disability requiring accommodation, so long as they are not used to constitute a quorum and are not permitted to be a deciding vote on a motion. Additionally, if a board member is participating remotely because of a military duty absence or reasonable accommodation for a disability, other board members may not contribute remotely unless a military duty or reasonable accommodation exception applies. A footnote elaborates that this approach carries legal risk: MCL 15.263a(1) allows board meetings to be held electronically, in whole or in part, consistent with that section and remaining OMA obligations, and MCL 15.263a(8) explicitly states that meetings held under MCL 15.263a must be carried out to only allow members with a military duty absence to participate electronically. In theory, if no members are attending due to a military absence leave, then so long as board members who contribute remotely are not counted to establish a quorum or used to decide a vote, those members do not create even a partially "electronic" meeting under the OMA. The footnote adds that as a practical matter clients adopting this approach are unlikely to face significant liability even if a court definitively decided the policy violated the OMA, since members are still not counted toward a quorum or allowed to be a deciding voter and can simply give their opinions; while there is some legal risk and liability, including payment of attorney's fees in a legal action, the firm would not anticipate members of the public initiating legal action based on such a minor potential violation.

RECOMMENDATION. Clients are advised to adopt one of two policies. Option A is intended for those who wish to reduce legal risk and/or do not wish to actively monitor which board members will participate remotely and to what degree. Option B is intended for those who wish to allow board members more flexibility in attending remotely but understand that doing so could create legal risk and liability if successfully challenged in court.

OPTION A TEXT. "Electronic Meetings and Remote Participation. A Board member must be physically present at the meeting to participate in a meeting as a Board member, except as otherwise permitted by the OMA." If a Board member participates remotely because of an absence due to military duty, or as the only reasonable accommodation available for a disability that would otherwise prevent attendance, the following conditions must be met: in addition to any other notice required under the OMA, the Board must post advance notice consistent with MCL 15.263a(4) and post the agenda consistent with MCL 15.263a(5); the Board Secretary must include the name of each Board member attending remotely in the meeting minutes, and an announcement must be made at the outset of the meeting that the member is attending remotely, and except for a member absent due to military duty the announcement must also identify the member's specific location by state and city, township, county, or village; the Board must use 2-way communication so that remote members can hear and be heard by other Board members and public participants; the remote member must notify the Board President at least one (1) business day before the meeting so the President can arrange to notify the general public of the means by which it may contact the member prior to the meeting; and the Board President must take steps to ensure the general public is aware of the manner any remote member voted on any and all matters brought before the Board for a vote, such as requiring roll call voting.

OPTION B TEXT. "Electronic Meetings and Remote Participation. A Board member must be physically present at the meeting to be counted toward a quorum or vote in a meeting, except as otherwise permitted by the OMA." Board members who are not explicitly authorized under the OMA to participate remotely, or who do not have a disability for which the only reasonable accommodation is remote attendance, may remotely contribute to Board meetings; however, any such member may not be counted toward a quorum or vote in such meeting. Additionally, if any Board member is present remotely due to a reason explicitly authorized by the OMA or as reasonable accommodation for a disability, no other Board member may remotely contribute unless they are present remotely due to military duty or reasonable accommodation for a disability. Option B then repeats the same five bulleted conditions as Option A for members participating remotely due to military duty or disability accommodation. A footnote to Option B notes that the bullet-list of conditions applicable to remote meetings accommodating a military absence or disability is not required when the voting and present members are all present physically and the members who are not "present" are merely contributing remotely.

The memo closes by inviting questions regarding the suggested revisions at Policy@MillerJohnson.com.

**Framework**
Project 2026 Blueprint - Troy School District. The World Class for All pillars are aligned to the core values of Collaboration, Deep Learning and Focus, and the Accountability Plan holds the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results. Four pillars: Green (Early Childhood to Career), Red (Equity and Well-Being), Blue (Deep Learning) and Gold (Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families).

**Green Pillar - Early Childhood to Career**
Objectives: continue investing in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for universal preschool access for all three- and four-year-olds; expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students, broadening access to computer science and career and technical education and connecting underrepresented students to in-demand careers through partnerships with higher education institutions and employers. Key Results (updated October 2022) include early childhood recruitment for 2022-23, transition from preschool to kindergarten, monitoring preschool impact on achievement data, building leaders participating twice in Career Readiness meetings during 2021-22, the Portrait of a Graduate work with Tony Wagner, and preparation for digital portfolios tied to Xello.

June-November 2022 celebrations, early childhood enrollment at a record high of 483:

| Program | Enrollment | TSD share |
|---|---|---|
| Tuition | 271 | 88% TSD |
| GSRP | 80 | 91% TSD |
| PreK | 67 | 100% TSD |
| ECP | 65 | 100% TSD |

Challenges: capacity limit for early childhood programs, barriers to preschool access, alignment of Media/Maker with Career Readiness, the stigma of career readiness, and balancing Portrait of a Graduate against current priorities. November 2022 recommendations: a January 11, 2023 Preschool Information Night, prioritized career readiness messaging, an LTU partnership for early middle college adoption, and Portrait of a Graduate.

**Red Pillar - Equity and Well-Being**
Objectives cover wraparound services and hiring more counselors, social workers and school psychologists, and assessing the need for upgraded facilities. Key Results include increased social work and counseling support, recruitment of a new Supervisor of Equity and Inclusion, A.L.I.C.E. 2-day administrator training, classroom safety buckets, and administrator safety tabletop exercises. January-June 2023 work includes a Middle School Advisory Study Team, Student Code of Conduct Review Team, expansion of the District/TEA Professional Relations Committee, and a book study on Culturally Responsive Teaching & The Brain.

**Blue Pillar - Deep Learning and assessment update**
Objectives cover MTSS, technology access, global best practices (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships) and facilities. Key Results include Math Recovery training, elementary and middle school math pilots, digital portfolios, and elementary and secondary MTSS work. The embedded Student Achievement Update 2022 Fall Assessment Review explains M-STEP (grades 3-8 and 11, begun 2015, computer adaptive in ELA and math), PSAT 8/9 and PSAT 10, and the Michigan Merit Exam for grade 11 (M-STEP science and social studies, SAT with Essay, ACT WorkKeys). MI-Access: TSD tested 66 students in 2022. WIDA: TSD tested 1,839 students in 2022. Performance levels are not proficient, partially proficient, proficient and advanced. The Class of 2023 had a required 8th grade test, optional 10th grade test and required 11th grade test; the Class of 2024 is shown as testing optional.

**Gold Pillar - Building Capacity**
Objectives address educator preparation, pipelines for underrepresented educators and job-embedded professional learning for the OneTroy community. Key Results include rebranding the Health Care Aide position as Student Support Aide, a new "Sub-Cabinet" team, and expanded partnerships with OU (secondary), EMU (special education) and WSU (social work). Challenges: teacher coverage for job-embedded learning, calendar time for collaboration, finding candidates with diverse backgrounds, and teacher shortage particularly in special education.

**Redesign process**
See, Engage, Act: SEE uses system level, demographic, process, academic and perception data; ENGAGE runs listening sessions with students, BOE, parents and all staff in February, March and April; ACT redesigns with the Strategic Planning Team, reviews with the BOE, finalizes Strategic Planning 2025 in May, and sets next steps in bond planning.

Board accountability presentation for the Troy School District's Project 2026 Blueprint, presented with slide date stamps of 10/20/22. The deck opens with CORE VALUES, stating that the World Class for All Pillars are carefully aligned to the District's core values of Collaboration, Deep Learning and Focus, and with an ACCOUNTABILITY PLAN slide stating that the World Class for All Pillars hold the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results. GREEN PILLAR - EARLY CHILDHOOD TO CAREER, OBJECTIVES. Continue to invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for access to universal preschool for all three and four-year-olds. Expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students; the plan aims to provide more students with access to high-quality career and technical education programs that expand access to computer science, and to connect underrepresented students to careers in demand in high-growth industry sectors, including partnerships with institutions of higher education, employers and other stakeholders that allow students to engage in quality work-based learning opportunities, earn a credential, and/or earn college credit.

GREEN PILLAR KEY RESULTS (updated October 2022). Early childhood recruitment for 2022-23 early and frequent. Focus on meaningful transition from Preschool to Kindergarten, with monitoring of the impact of preschool on achievement data and monitoring of access across the district. Building leaders will participate in Career Readiness meetings, led by district CR team leaders, and report back to their respective building teams two times during the 2021-22 school year. On Portrait of a Graduate (POG), the Board of Education met with Tony Wagner, along with the community, to discuss and validate POG importance to overall student success in post-secondary preparation. Preparation for digital portfolios with K-5 media staff, middle school innovation coaches and 6-8 English teachers, tied to Xello and future-ready exit discussions with students.

GREEN PILLAR JUNE-NOVEMBER 2022 CELEBRATIONS. Current Early Childhood Enrollment at a record high of 483, comprising Tuition 271 (88% TSD), GSRP 80 (91% TSD), PreK 67 (100% TSD) and ECP 65 (100% TSD). Growth and access data include Fountas and Pinnell impact of preschool over time and preschool experience by TSD elementary building. Also cited: Kindergarten Transition Committee, enhanced spring transition opportunities, Portrait of a Graduate work with Tony Wagner including an August session with the Board of Education and two October community sessions, career readiness engagement opportunities in K-5 partnered with Media Specialists and Maker Space growth, and continued prioritization of post-secondary learning partnerships throughout K-12.

GREEN PILLAR JUNE-NOVEMBER 2022 CHALLENGES. Capacity limit for early childhood programs; identifying barriers to preschool access; alignment of Media/Maker with Career Readiness in terms of time and consistency; mindshifting the stigma of career readiness to help prioritize relevance to classroom learning; and balancing Portrait of a Graduate with current top priorities.

GREEN PILLAR NOVEMBER 2022 RECOMMENDATIONS. January 11, 2023 Preschool Information Night for recruitment; prioritize messaging career readiness as a tool for students aligned with academic planning and college readiness among administrators, teachers and counselors; develop a partnership with LTU for the early middle college adoption process; and Portrait of a Graduate.

RED PILLAR - EQUITY AND WELL-BEING, OBJECTIVES. Ensure a focus on equity and well-being by funding additional investments to support the needs of the whole child, including community schools providing wraparound services such as afterschool programs, and hiring more counselors, social workers and school psychologists; and assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.

RED PILLAR KEY RESULTS. Increase social work and counseling support in all buildings; review and monitor student data; emphasis on adult learning in areas of well-being and equity; recruit and hire a new Supervisor of Equity and Inclusion; A.L.I.C.E. two-day administrator training; classroom safety buckets deployed; and administrator safety "tabletop" exercises.

RED PILLAR JANUARY-JUNE 2023. Middle School Advisory Study Team; Student Code of Conduct Review Team; expand the District/TEA Professional Relations Committee; book study on Culturally Responsive Teaching & The Brain; review and monitor student data, with data reviews conducted and interventions in progress; emphasis on adult learning in well-being and equity through monthly staff topics; create common understanding of a system of support at all levels, with a District Level Team established.

BLUE PILLAR - DEEP LEARNING, OBJECTIVES. Create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice (MTSS), on the premise that access to deep learning is imperative for all children; improve technology access for students and families while providing quality training to leverage technology to deepen learning; continue to pursue global best practices in all content areas (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships); and assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities.

BLUE PILLAR KEY RESULTS. Elementary Resource and Teacher Consultants trained in Math Recovery Training; elementary and middle school math pilots rooted in professional learning partnerships; begin to develop digital portfolios for students to document learning over time; elementary Media team continuing to develop curriculum using inquiry and maker-centered practices with secondary engaged in this learning; elementary MTSS continuing to monitor benchmark data and develop capacity in math; and secondary MTSS continuing to define roles on the MTSS team and consider data to be utilized.

STUDENT ACHIEVEMENT UPDATE 2022 - FALL ASSESSMENT REVIEW. The deck explains how Michigan measures progress: once each spring all students take the state assessment(s); M-STEP is given each spring to students in grades 3-8; the PSAT (PreSAT) is given each spring to students in grades 8 and 9 (PSAT 8/9) and 10 (PSAT 10); and the Michigan Merit Exam (MME) comprises a suite of tests for students in grade 11 including the SAT. Certain populations take uniquely designed assessments: MI-Access is given each spring to students whose Individualized Education Program (IEP) team has determined that general assessments, even with accommodations, are not appropriate, and TSD tested 66 students in 2022; the WIDA program of assessments is given each spring to English learners, and TSD tested 1,839 students in 2022. State standardized assessments are required under both state and federal law to ensure all children are learning and receiving a high-quality education, and are summative, measuring what students are expected to know and be able to do at specific grade levels and in specific content areas.

M-STEP is aligned to Michigan's learning standards and is administered each spring to students in grades 3-8 and 11; it began in 2015 and measures skills in English language arts, mathematics, social studies and science, with the note that students in grades 8 and 11 take M-STEP for social studies and science only. M-STEP assessments in ELA and mathematics use computer adaptive testing (CAT), customized for each student. The Michigan Department of Education provides the PSAT for students in grades 8, 9 and 10; for grade 8 students, PSAT 8/9 replaces M-STEP tests in ELA and mathematics, while M-STEP science and social studies continue to be administered in grade 8. The MME for 11th grade students includes three components: M-STEP assessments in science and social studies; the SAT with Essay, a college admission test that also measures student knowledge of state standards in ELA and mathematics; and ACT WorkKeys work skills measurement. Student performance is described as one of four levels: not proficient, partially proficient, proficient and advanced. Because M-STEP is a very different state test than those administered prior to spring 2015, results should not be compared to MEAP results through 2014; similarly, because PSAT 8/9 differs significantly from M-STEP ELA and mathematics tests, year-to-year comparisons of grade 8 ELA and mathematics results should wait until 2020 and beyond. A data review section notes testing status by cohort: Class of 2023 - required 8th grade, optional 10th grade, required 11th grade; Class of 2024 - testing optional.

(RE)DESIGN PROCESS: SEE, ENGAGE, ACT. SEE draws on system level data, demographic, process, academic and perception data. ENGAGE consists of listening sessions and planning with students, the BOE, parents and all staff during February, March and April. ACT covers redesign with the Strategic Planning Team, review with the BOE, finalizing Strategic Planning 2025 in May, and next steps in bond planning.

GOLD PILLAR - BUILDING CAPACITY OF STUDENTS, STAFF, AND FAMILIES, OBJECTIVES. Improving educator preparation, strengthening pipelines for underrepresented educators, and supporting current educators; continue to provide job-embedded professional learning experiences for all staff; and provide professional learning opportunities for staff, community and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community.

GOLD PILLAR KEY RESULTS. Rebranding of the Health Care Aide position to Student Support Aide; Student Support Aide orientation, mentoring and training process; Services/CO/Secretarial staff collaboration and training sessions; creation of a new "Sub-Cabinet" Team; expanded partnerships with OU (secondary), EMU (special education) and WSU (social work); and successful teacher retention. A staff recognition element lists years-of-service tiers of 15+, 20+ and 25+ years. Further key results: create a Teaching & Learning workplan for 100% of secondary staff to have a job-embedded experience; elementary resource room teachers and teacher consultants trained in Math Recovery and secondary math specialists trained in Math Recovery; host a parent learning series around deep learning and well-being; expand the Teachers College Partnership to include high school; math pilot work at middle school rooted in professional learning partnerships; and utilize late-start days to prioritize conversations with collaborative teacher teams around student learning.

GOLD PILLAR CHALLENGES. Teacher coverage for job-embedded learning; need for time built into the calendar for teacher collaboration; finding candidates with diverse backgrounds who want to apply or relocate for positions in the area; and teacher shortage, particularly in special education.

2022_287_november_22_23_accountability_p.page:
**Deck**
Project 2026 Blueprint - Troy School District, November 2022-23 Accountability Plan, 41 slides. Core values: Collaboration, Deep Learning, Focus. The Accountability Plan holds the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results across four pillars: Green (Early Childhood to Career), Red (Equity and Well-Being), Blue (Deep Learning) and Gold (Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families).

**Green Pillar - Early Childhood to Career**
Objectives: continue investing in high-quality early childhood education including advocacy for universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds; expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students through CTE and computer science access, connecting underrepresented students to in-demand careers via partnerships with higher education institutions and employers for work-based learning, credentials and college credit. Key Results (updated October 2022): early and frequent 2022-23 early childhood recruitment; preschool-to-kindergarten transition; monitoring preschool impact on achievement data and access across the district; building leaders participating twice in Career Readiness meetings during 2021-22; Portrait of a Graduate work with Tony Wagner; and digital portfolio preparation with K-5 media, middle school innovation coaches and 6-8 English teachers tied to Xello.

June-November 2022 celebrations, early childhood enrollment at a record high of 483:

| Program | Enrollment | TSD share |
|---|---|---|
| Tuition | 271 | 88% TSD |
| GSRP | 80 | 91% TSD |
| PreK | 67 | 100% TSD |
| ECP | 65 | 100% TSD |

A narrative slide reports that a preschool experience results in an ELA advantage sustained through 5th grade, with children without preschool 2-3 times more likely to be below grade level, though interventions reduce that gap over time; COVID increased the number of kindergartners arriving without that experience, reversing a 4-year positive trend, and record preschool enrollment suggests that number will drop again next year.

Challenges: early childhood capacity limits, barriers to preschool access, Media/Maker alignment with Career Readiness, career-readiness stigma, and balancing Portrait of a Graduate. November 2022 recommendations: January 11, 2023 Preschool Information Night; prioritized career readiness messaging; LTU partnership for early middle college adoption; Portrait of a Graduate.

**Red Pillar - Equity and Well-Being**
Objectives: fund investments supporting the whole child, including community schools with wraparound services such as afterschool programs and hiring more counselors, social workers and school psychologists; assess and act on facility upgrades. Key Results: increased social work and counseling support, student data review, adult learning on well-being and equity, recruiting a Supervisor of Equity and Inclusion, A.L.I.C.E. 2-day administrator training, classroom safety buckets, and administrator tabletop exercises. January-June 2023: Middle School Advisory Study Team, Student Code of Conduct Review Team, expanded District/TEA Professional Relations Committee, book study on Culturally Responsive Teaching & The Brain, District Level Team established. Recommendations: continued social work, psychologist and counseling support; resource implementation; monthly staff topics and district-wide equity learning; equity data analysis; SEL pilots for 2022-23; and development of a district level Equity Leader network.

**Blue Pillar - Deep Learning and assessment review**
Objectives: MTSS systems of support and student voice; improved technology access and training; global best practices (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships); facility upgrades. Key Results: Math Recovery training for elementary resource and teacher consultants, elementary and middle school math pilots, digital portfolios, inquiry and maker-centered media curriculum, and elementary and secondary MTSS work. The embedded Student Achievement Update 2022 Fall Assessment Review covers M-STEP (grades 3-8 and 11, began 2015, computer adaptive in ELA and math), PSAT 8/9 and PSAT 10, and the MME for grade 11 (M-STEP science and social studies, SAT with Essay, ACT WorkKeys), with four performance levels and cautions against comparison to MEAP results through 2014. Data slides are titled PSAT8 by Math, PSAT8 & %ED, SAT by Math and SAT & %ED.

**Gold Pillar - Building Capacity**
Objectives: improve educator preparation, strengthen pipelines for underrepresented educators, support current educators, provide job-embedded professional learning, and co-design experiences for the OneTroy community. Key Results: Student Support Aide rebranding and training, staff collaboration sessions, a new "Sub-Cabinet" Team, expanded partnerships with OU (secondary), EMU (special education) and WSU (social work), successful teacher retention, a T&L workplan for 100% of secondary staff, Math Recovery training, a parent learning series, expanded Teachers College Partnership including high school, middle school math pilots, and use of late-start days. Challenges: teacher coverage for job-embedded learning, calendar time for collaboration, recruiting candidates with diverse backgrounds, and teacher shortage particularly in special education.

**Redesign process**
See, Engage, Act: system level, demographic, process, academic and perception data; listening sessions with students, BOE, parents and all staff in February, March and April; redesign with the Strategic Planning Team, BOE review, finalizing Strategic Planning 2025 in May, and next steps in bond planning.

November 2022-23 Accountability Plan presentation for the Troy School District's Project 2026 Blueprint, a 41-slide deck. Slide 1 identifies the Project 2026 Blueprint at district and school levels. Slide 2, CORE VALUES, states that the World Class for All Pillars are carefully aligned to the core values of Collaboration, Deep Learning and Focus. Slide 3, ACCOUNTABILITY PLAN, states that the World Class for All Pillars hold the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results. The pillars are color-coded: Green for Early Childhood to Career, Red for Equity and Well-Being, Blue for Deep Learning, and Gold for Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families.

GREEN PILLAR OBJECTIVES (Slide 4). Continue to invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for access to universal preschool for all three and four-year-olds. Expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students; the plan aims to provide more students with access to high-quality career and technical education programs that expand access to computer science, and to connect underrepresented students to careers in demand in high-growth industry sectors, including partnerships with institutions of higher education, employers and other stakeholders that allow students to engage in quality work-based learning opportunities, earn a credential, and/or earn college credit.

GREEN PILLAR KEY RESULTS, UPDATED OCTOBER 2022 (Slide 5). Early childhood recruitment for 2022-23 early and frequent. Focus on meaningful transition from Preschool to Kindergarten, with monitoring of the impact of preschool on achievement data and monitoring of access across the district. Building leaders will participate in Career Readiness meetings, led by district CR team leaders, and report back to their respective building teams two times during the 2021-22 school year. On Portrait of a Graduate, the Board of Education met with Tony Wagner, along with the community, to discuss and validate POG importance to overall student success in post-secondary preparation. Preparation for digital portfolios with K-5 media, middle school innovation coaches and 6-8 English teachers, tied to Xello and future-ready exit discussions with students.

GREEN PILLAR JUNE-NOVEMBER 2022 CELEBRATIONS (Slide 6). Current Early Childhood Enrollment at a record high of 483: Tuition 271 (88% TSD), GSRP 80 (91% TSD), PreK 67 (100% TSD), and ECP 65 (100% TSD). Growth and access data include F & P impact of preschool over time and preschool experience by TSD elementary building. Also listed: Kindergarten Transition Committee, enhanced spring transition opportunities, Portrait of a Graduate with Tony Wagner including an August session with the Board of Education and two October community sessions, career readiness engagement opportunities in K-5 partnered with Media Specialists and Maker Space growth, and continued prioritization of post-secondary learning partnerships throughout K-12.

PRESCHOOL IMPACT NARRATIVE (Slide 7). "A preschool experience results in an ELA advantage sustained through 5th grade: kids without preschool were 2-3 times more likely to be below grade level (although our interventions reduce that gap over time). Note that COVID increased the number of our Kindergarteners arriving this year without that experience, reversing a 4-year positive trend. Record enrollees in our Preschool this year would suggest that number will drop again next year."

GREEN PILLAR JUNE-NOVEMBER 2022 CHALLENGES (Slide 8). Capacity limit for early childhood programs; identifying barriers to preschool access; alignment of Media/Maker with Career Readiness in time and consistency; mindshifting the stigma of career readiness to help prioritize relevance to classroom learning; and balancing Portrait of a Graduate with current top priorities.

GREEN PILLAR NOVEMBER 2022 RECOMMENDATIONS (Slide 9). January 11, 2023 Preschool Information Night for recruitment; prioritize messaging career readiness as a tool for students aligned with academic planning and college readiness with administrators, teachers and counselors; develop a partnership with LTU for the early middle college adoption process; and Portrait of a Graduate.

RED PILLAR OBJECTIVES (Slide 10). Ensuring a focus on Equity and Well-Being: fund additional investments to support the needs of the whole child, including community schools that provide wraparound services like afterschool programs, and hiring more counselors, social workers and school psychologists; assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.

RED PILLAR KEY RESULTS (Slide 11). Increase social work and counseling support in all buildings; review and monitor student data; emphasis on adult learning in areas of well-being and equity; recruit and hire a new Supervisor of Equity and Inclusion; A.L.I.C.E. two-day administrator training; classroom safety buckets deployed; and administrator safety "tabletop" exercises.

RED PILLAR JANUARY-JUNE 2023 (Slide 12). Middle School Advisory Study Team; Student Code of Conduct Review Team; expand District/TEA Professional Relations Committee; book study on Culturally Responsive Teaching & The Brain; review and monitor student data, with data reviews conducted and interventions in progress; emphasis on adult learning in well-being and equity via monthly staff topics; and create common understanding of a system of support at all levels, with a District Level Team established.

RED PILLAR RECOMMENDATIONS (Slide 13). Continue social work, psychologist and counseling support in all buildings; review and monitor student data with resource implementation for support; emphasis on adult learning in well-being and equity through monthly staff topics, district-wide learning on equity, and evaluating progress and future goals through equity data analysis; create common understanding of a system of support at all levels with SEL pilots for 2022-23; and development of a district level Equity Leader network.

BLUE PILLAR OBJECTIVES (Slide 14). Create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice (MTSS), noting access to deep learning is imperative for all children; improve technology access for students and families while providing quality training to leverage technology to deepen learning; continue to pursue the global best practices of all content areas (NPDL, The 6 C's, learning partnerships); and assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.

BLUE PILLAR KEY RESULTS (Slide 15). Elementary Resource and Teacher Consultants trained in Math Recovery Training; elementary and middle school math pilots rooted in professional learning partnerships; begin to develop digital portfolios for students to document learning over time; elementary Media team continuing to develop curriculum using inquiry and maker-centered practices with secondary engaged in this learning; elementary MTSS continuing to monitor benchmark data and develop capacity in math; and secondary MTSS continuing to define roles on the MTSS team and consider data to be utilized.

STUDENT ACHIEVEMENT UPDATE 2022 - FALL ASSESSMENT REVIEW (Slides 16-35). How Michigan measures progress: once each spring, all students take the state assessment(s); M-STEP is given each spring to students in grades 3-8; the PSAT (PreSAT) is given each spring to students in grades 8, 9 (PSAT 8/9) and 10 (PSAT 10); and the Michigan Merit Exam comprises a suite of tests for students in grade 11 including the SAT. A slide asks "Why State Assessments?" and two slides present Michigan's Assessment System at a Glance, including the state assessment for students with significant cognitive impairment and state assessments for English learners. M-STEP is aligned to Michigan's learning standards and administered each spring to students in grades 3-8 and 11; it began in 2015 and measures skills in English language arts, mathematics, social studies and science, with students in grades 8 and 11 taking M-STEP for social studies and science only. M-STEP assessments in ELA and mathematics use computer adaptive testing (CAT), customized for each student. The Michigan Department of Education provides the PSAT for students in grades 8, 9 and 10; for grade 8 students, PSAT 8/9 replaces M-STEP tests in ELA and mathematics, while M-STEP science and social studies continue in grade 8. The MME for 11th grade students includes three components: M-STEP assessments in science and social studies; the SAT with Essay, a college admission test that also measures student knowledge of state standards in ELA and mathematics; and ACT WorkKeys work skills measurement. Student performance is described as one of four levels: not proficient, partially proficient, proficient and advanced. Because M-STEP is a very different state test than those administered prior to spring 2015, results should not be compared to MEAP results through 2014; similarly, because PSAT 8/9 differs significantly from M-STEP ELA and mathematics tests, year-to-year comparisons of grade 8 ELA and mathematics results should wait until 2020 and beyond. A Data Review section follows, with chart slides titled PSAT8 by Math, PSAT8 & %ED, SAT by Math, and SAT & %ED.

(RE)DESIGN PROCESS: SEE, ENGAGE, ACT (Slide 36). SEE draws on system level data, demographic, process, academic and perception data. ENGAGE consists of listening sessions and planning with students, the BOE, parents and all staff during February, March and April. ACT covers redesign with the Strategic Planning Team, review with the BOE, finalizing Strategic Planning 2025 in May, and next steps in bond planning.

GOLD PILLAR OBJECTIVES (Slide 37). Improving educator preparation, strengthening pipelines for underrepresented educators, and supporting current educators; continue to provide job-embedded professional learning experiences for all staff; and provide professional learning opportunities for staff, community and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community.

GOLD PILLAR KEY RESULTS (Slides 38-39). Rebranding of the Health Care Aide position to Student Support Aide; Student Support Aide orientation, mentoring and training process; Services/CO/Secretarial staff collaboration and training sessions; creation of a new "Sub-Cabinet" Team; expanded partnerships with OU (secondary), EMU (special education) and WSU (social work); and successful teacher retention. Additional key results: create a Teaching & Learning workplan for 100% of secondary staff to have a job-embedded experience; elementary resource room and teacher consultants trained in Math Recovery and secondary math specialists trained in Math Recovery; host a parent learning series around deep learning and well-being; expand the Teachers College Partnership to include high school; math pilot work at middle school rooted in professional learning partnerships; and utilize late-start days to prioritize conversations with collaborative teacher teams around student learning.

GOLD PILLAR CHALLENGES (Slide 40). Teacher coverage for job-embedded learning; need for time built into the calendar for teacher collaboration; finding candidates with diverse backgrounds who want to apply or relocate for positions in the area; and teacher shortage, particularly in special education.
